overview: The U.S. Postal Service is led by the Postmaster General and a deputy, whose pay and bonuses are approved by the Postal Service's Board of Governors. This bill bars the board from approving any bonus or award beyond basic pay for either official in any year when the Postal Service fails to meet at least 95 percent on-time delivery for each of its delivery targets for core mail services, such as letters and first-class mail. Bonuses would also be blocked in any year when the Postal Service's financial deficit grows compared with the year before, or when it runs a deficit after having a surplus the year before. The bill also requires the Postal Service to send its annual performance report to the Postal Regulatory Commission, the independent agency that oversees it. As of September 14, 2026, it had been approved by a Senate committee and placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say top postal leaders shouldn't receive extra pay in years when mail service falls short or finances get worse, and tying bonuses to clear targets builds accountability.
against: Critics say the 95 percent on-time and deficit tests are strict, and many of the Postal Service's financial pressures come from factors leaders don't fully control, which could make it harder to attract and keep strong leadership.
